text: The head chef of a four-to-eight-site independent group. Every menu change or supplier substitution, which happens weekly and daily on specials, makes the printed allergen matrix wrong until someone re-checks it against the supplier spec sheets, and nobody does that the same day. The person who pays is a diner with an allergy who is told "no nuts" by a waiter reading a stale sheet. Frequency: the chefs admit to about one wrong matrix per site per month; how many diners are exposed per stale sheet is unknown, and that gap is itself the finding. Cost: at the top, a death and a corporate manslaughter case against the owner; at the median, an EHO improvement notice and a re-inspection; at the floor, the chef loses two to three hours a week re-typing a spreadsheet, and the group cannot show its insurer when the matrix was last correct.

Today it is a laminated matrix at the pass and a spreadsheet the head chef owns, rebuilt from supplier spec sheets that arrive as PDFs in email. The EPOS and the recipe-costing system both have an allergen field per dish; it was filled in once at menu launch and has not been touched since. Two of our sites tried a dedicated allergen tool; it needs every dish re-keyed by hand, so it died at the second menu change. The wholesaler's data feed covers packaged goods and nothing from the butcher, the bakery or Saturday's specials. The shortcomings are the same one three times over. The matrix is a snapshot, not a record: no timestamp, no name against a change, no way to show what was true on the day a diner reacted. The trigger for a change is a delivery or a substitution at the pass, and the person who sees it is not the person who edits the sheet. And "may contain" is handled by each chef's own judgement, so the same sauce is a nut risk at one site and not at another.

The documented process is four steps: menu change, chef updates the spreadsheet, manager prints and laminates the matrix, front of house is briefed at pre-shift. As it actually runs: the delivery arrives at seven and the kitchen porter signs the note; if the wholesaler has substituted a brand, that is where it enters the building, and nobody reads the substitution line. A sous chef may notice at prep, and tells the head chef verbally if the head chef is on. Specials go on the whiteboard at half eleven with no allergen line; the rule is "ask the kitchen". At the five o'clock briefing the manager reads the laminate for the set menu and repeats "ask the kitchen" for specials. When a diner asks, the waiter either reads the laminate, which may be a menu behind, or shouts to the pass, and the chef answers from memory mid-service. The only record of that exchange is "ALLERGY" written on the ticket, which goes in the bin at close. The head chef updates the spreadsheet on their day off, from memory, then prints it at whichever site has a working printer, so two sites usually run different versions. The EPOS field is never touched. When the EHO comes, the manager searches their email for spec sheets while the inspector waits.

Seven things, and I would test them in this order. One: a substitution can be captured where it enters the building, at the delivery note, by the porter who signs it, not by the chef; if the capture step depends on the chef it dies the way the spreadsheet died. Two: reading a spec sheet is accurate enough that a chef trusts it over their own memory, which means near-zero missed "contains" lines, and "may contain" decided once by a group policy rather than per chef. Three: the wholesaler feed plus PDF reading covers most ingredients, and the remainder from the butcher, the bakery and today's specials can be entered at the pass in under a minute. Four: the dishes import once from the recipe-costing system; nobody re-keys a menu. Five: front of house reads a screen, or the laminate reprints itself at every site the moment something changes. Six: the owner pays, because what they are buying is the timestamped record, not the matrix. Seven: an EHO and our insurer accept that record as the evidence, and say so before we build it.

The seven above are the conditions; the riskiest is the first one, capture at the delivery note. It asks for a behaviour change from the lowest-paid, highest-churn person in the building at seven in the morning, and every other condition is downstream of it: if substitutions do not enter the system on the day, the extraction accuracy, the auto-reprint and the record are all describing a matrix that is already wrong, and we have rebuilt the spreadsheet with nicer formatting. The other candidates are cheaper to retire. Extraction accuracy is a desk test against two hundred spec sheets in a week. Whether the owner pays is five conversations. Whether the EHO accepts a digital ledger is one phone call to the local authority. Capture needs a live site for a month. So the test is two sites, four weeks, porters photograph every delivery note, and we count substitutions captured against the wholesaler's own substitution log as ground truth. Under eighty percent and the capture point moves off the porter before anything else gets built.

Not the same person, and the gap is the whole design problem. The pain day to day is the head chef's: the Monday rebuild, and being shouted at from the floor mid-service to answer from memory. The waiter feels it in the moment they say "no nuts" without knowing. The diner carries the risk and is nobody's customer. The budget is the owner's, or the ops director's in the larger groups, and they feel nothing until the EHO visit or the phone call from a solicitor, which is the one day pain and budget sit in the same chair and it is too late to buy anything. So the chef will not champion a tool that adds a step, and the owner will not pay for the chef's convenience. What the owner will pay for is the record: proof of what was true on a given day. That is why condition one puts the capture on the porter and not the chef, and why the product has to cost the kitchen zero extra steps to be adopted while being sold upstairs as liability cover. The broker who renews the group's insurance may be the buyer's buyer; that is worth one conversation before we price it.

Not a quick fix. A quick fix here is a better spreadsheet template, which is what the two sites that tried the dedicated tool effectively bought, and it died at the second menu change. It is a big idea, but the appetite is not "the product", it is one six-week cycle with two people on the spine only: delivery-note capture at the porter, a substitution ledger with a name and a timestamp against every change, the per-dish matrix derived from that ledger, and the laminate reprinting itself at every site. The four-week capture test from the last question runs first with phones and a shared sheet, so the cycle starts knowing whether the porter step holds. Fixed time, variable scope: if it runs long, the first thing cut is automatic spec-sheet reading, which degrades to a chef typing the allergen line from the PDF, and the last thing cut is the timestamped record, because that is the thing the owner is paying for. We would not redesign anything we already have. The EPOS and the costing system stay as they are and we import dishes from them once; the day we ask a chef to re-key a menu we have lost.

New work: yes, one piece. Reading a photographed delivery note at seven in the morning, wet, folded, with the substitution written by hand, is not something we have done; spec-sheet PDFs are close to work we know. The wholesaler feed is an unknown format but a known kind of job. Parts fitting together: the assumption nobody has drawn is the matching layer. The note says "Pesto Genovese 1kg, brand B", the recipe says "pesto", and the costing system may say something else again; if supplier product names cannot be tied to recipe ingredients reliably, the ledger records substitutions that never reach a dish. That is a rabbit hole and it needs a spike before the cycle. Assumed design: two places. Entering a special at the pass in under a minute, and a front-of-house screen a waiter uses mid-service with a diner waiting; neither exists yet and we should not assume they are easy. Hard decisions to settle now: first, "may contain" is treated as "contains" for the matrix, decided once for the group, because it changes the data model and every dish's status. Second, a porter's photo creates a pending change that marks the affected dishes "unverified" on the floor until a chef confirms; it does not wait silently for the chef, or condition one is back on the chef's shoulders.

Out of bounds for this cycle, taken from the rabbit holes just named. Automatic spec-sheet reading: a chef types the allergen line from the PDF; reading it comes in a later cycle if capture holds. The wholesaler feed: manual until we have seen three real formats. The front-of-house screen: the laminate reprints itself; a tablet at the till is the next bet, not this one. Writing back into the EPOS or the costing system: import only, ever. Anything diner-facing, including a QR allergen menu, because publishing to the diner changes who is liable for a wrong line and we have not had that conversation with the insurer. Natasha's Law labels for packaged food: adjacent, tempting, no. Nutrition and costing: not ours. More than one group: one group, its sites, one policy. And one permanent boundary rather than a cycle boundary: the product never answers "is this safe for me". It records what is in a dish and who last confirmed it; the chef answers the diner.

Legally, the food business operator, meaning the owner's company, is accountable today and stays accountable; our design does not move that and must not claim to. In practice the blame lands on the waiter who said "no nuts" and the chef who answered from memory, and the porter who signed the substitution is never in the frame. Our design does change the practical picture, and I want to say that plainly rather than discover it in a disciplinary. A ledger with a name and a time against every change makes blame precise: a chef who left a dish "unverified" for three days is now visible, and so is a waiter who read an unverified line and answered anyway. That precision is what the owner is buying and it is why the chef will not love it, which is the Q6 problem again. Three commitments follow. The system never says "safe"; it says what is recorded and who last confirmed it, and the chef's confirmation is the act of record. We are accountable for the record being faithful, meaning what was entered is what is shown and nothing is altered after the fact, not for whether the chef was right. And nobody, including the owner, can edit history; the moment the owner can tidy the ledger before an inspector sees it, it is worthless as evidence and becomes a blame tool instead.

Four results, each with a date, and one with no date. First, the capture test: if porters capture under eighty percent of substitutions in four weeks and moving the capture point to the driver or the wholesaler's feed does not get it over eighty percent by the end of October, we stop, because a ledger nobody feeds is the spreadsheet again. Second, adoption: four weeks after the cycle ships to two sites, if the laminate on either wall is not the system's own print, meaning someone went back to the spreadsheet, we stop; date, nineteenth of December. Third, the money: if fewer than three of the five group owners we pitch will pay sixty pounds a site a month for the record, or the broker says a timestamped ledger moves nothing on premium or on their view of due diligence, the "owner buys the record" thesis is dead and so is the product; same date. Fourth, the authority: if our local EHO says in writing that a digital ledger is not an acceptable record, we stop before the cycle starts. And the one with no date: a diner reacts at a pilot site and our record was wrong about that dish. We stop that day and work out why before anything else.

There are three model steps and each gets its own eval: the delivery-note photo to a substitution line, the spec-sheet PDF to the fourteen flags plus may-contain, and the match from a supplier product name to a recipe ingredient. The set is ours, not a benchmark: two hundred spec sheets from our real suppliers including the scanned, multi-page, footnoted ones, the hundred or so delivery-note photos the capture test produces, and every product-to-ingredient pair on the flagship site's menu, each labelled independently by two head chefs so we also know how often the chefs disagree with each other, which is the ceiling on what "correct" can mean. The owner of the eval is the flagship head chef, because it is their judgement the system stands in for, and they run it, not the engineers. Pass rate is asymmetric. A missed "contains" is a diner; the pass bar is zero on the set, and one miss fails the release. A false positive costs a chef one confirmation, so up to five percent is acceptable. The match step passes at ninety-five percent with every unmatched line surfacing as "unverified" rather than dropped. It is run against the whole pipeline, not the model in isolation, re-run on every supplier change and every model change, and the number goes to the owner monthly, because it is their name on the record.

Winning aspiration: that an independent restaurant group can prove what was in any dish on any day, and no diner is ever answered from a stale sheet. Where we play: UK independent full-service groups of four to twenty sites, cooking their own recipes, buying from wholesalers. Not single sites, where there is no budget and no distance between owner and chef; not the big chains, which have compliance teams and bespoke systems; not quick-service, where the menu does not move. How we win: everyone else sells a matrix to the chef; we sell the record to the owner. The ledger is fed at the delivery note by the porter, not the chef, so it costs the kitchen nothing; it cannot be edited after the fact, so it counts as evidence; and it reaches the owner through the broker who renews the insurance. Capabilities that must exist: reading bad photographs of delivery notes, the product-to-ingredient matching layer, an append-only ledger, a group-level may-contain policy, working relationships with three regional wholesalers and two brokers. Management systems: one operating number per site, the capture rate; the eval run monthly by a chef and reported to the owner; the kill dates from the last answers reviewed on the day they fall, not after; and a rule that no history is ever edited, enforced in the software, not the handbook.

The capture test passed at eighty-two percent in October, because the porters knew they were being watched. We shipped in November. By February the flagship porter had left and the new one was never shown the photo step, so capture at that site fell to about half, and nobody noticed because the operating number was reported monthly and the site's chef said it was fine. The unverified flags piled up, and by March the chefs had learned to clear them in one go every Monday without opening a single change; the confirmation was a click, and the ledger looked pristine. Meanwhile the laminate now carried a time and a name, so front of house trusted it more than they had ever trusted the old one, and stopped shouting to the pass. In June a diner reacted at site three to a pesto the wholesaler had substituted in April. The ledger showed the chef had confirmed that dish at nine in the morning that day. The record we had sold as protection was the first exhibit against the chef, and the second against the owner, whose system had known. The broker, whom we had spoken to once and never in writing, said the ledger had no bearing on the policy. The chef was dismissed; the two other groups that had signed cancelled that week; and we had spent the spring building the spec-sheet reader we had declared out of bounds, because it was the interesting problem. The causes were four. We measured capture while people were watched. We let a confirmation be a click that showed nothing. We raised trust in the sheet faster than we raised its truth. And the conversation that made the whole thing worth paying for never happened on paper.

Yes, at least four, and two of them are not software. One: fix it at the source with a contract term. The wholesaler does not substitute without a phone call to the chef, and a paid hour on Monday's rota is the matrix check; cheapest by far, and it removes the porter from the problem entirely, but it depends on a supplier's goodwill and dies with the account manager. Two: build for the wholesaler, not the restaurant. They already hold the product data and the substitution log; a flag on their portal that says "this sub changes allergens" reaches every customer at once, and they have budgets. Different buyer, far fewer of them, and probably the better business. Three: go through the insurer. The broker mandates a record format and offers a premium reduction; the product becomes a template and a quarterly audit, not live software. Four: shrink the surface. Freeze specials, simplify recipes, fewer suppliers; that is a design constraint the owner can impose tomorrow for nothing. Our ledger is the fifth. I would take it, with option one written into the wholesaler contract alongside it, and I would keep option two as the pivot: if owners will not pay sixty pounds a site, the wholesaler is who we talk to next.

The last time was a Tuesday in March at site two. The thread is the "Kitchen, all sites" WhatsApp group: the sous chef posted a photo of a new pesto tub at 7.40 with "this one's cashew not pine nut, heads up", two thumbs up from other chefs, nothing from the head chef, who was off. That is the whole notification system. The file is "Allergen matrix v7 FINAL (2).xlsx" in the head chef's personal Google Drive, last modified in January, two months before the pesto; site two's laminate on the wall is v6. The spec sheet for the new pesto is in the head chef's inbox, found by searching "spec" and scrolling, sent by the wholesaler's account manager as an attachment with no message body. The tab open on the manager's laptop at site one from the May inspection is the FSA allergen guidance PDF, opened the morning the inspector was due, plus phone photos of the binder pages the inspector asked for. What was actually done: the sous chef changed the whiteboard by hand, told the floor verbally at five, and the head chef rebuilt the sheet at home on the Sunday, eleven days later. Nothing about the substitution exists anywhere except that WhatsApp photo, which will scroll off the group in a fortnight.

A Thursday in June, about eight in the evening, site three. A regular with a tree-nut allergy ordered the pasta with the pesto. The waiter checked the laminate, which was v6 from January and said pine nut, so she said "no nuts", and the ticket went to the pass with nothing on it. The chef on the pass had seen the March WhatsApp about the cashew pesto, remembered it, and pulled the plate. I heard about it two days later from the site manager, told as a good story: "great catch by Marco". That was the moment. The catch was one man's memory of a photo from three months earlier, on a night he happened to be on. I drove over, looked at the laminate on the wall, and it was v6. I asked the manager to show me what was true about that dish on that Thursday and nobody could, not the chef, not the sheet, not the EPOS. The next morning I rang the broker to ask what we were covered for, and the first thing she asked was "what's your allergen record", and I had no answer. Nothing had gone wrong, which is why it landed; I had been relying on luck and had just been shown the size of it.

It has been built, in the form that could be built: a matrix tool with the chef typing everything, which is what our two sites tried and abandoned. Three things are different now. First, reading a folded delivery note from a phone photo, and a footnoted spec-sheet PDF, costs pennies and is good enough to be checked rather than done by hand; two years ago the capture step needed a human typing, so every tool put the chef in the loop, and the chef is the one person who cannot carry it. Second, the enforcement posture changed after 2021: Natasha's Law and the prosecutions that followed turned allergens from a hygiene-rating footnote into something an owner personally fears, and brokers have started asking for the record at renewal. Third, the wholesalers digitised during the pandemic; the substitution log now exists as data somewhere, even if it is only ever printed. The honest other half is that the vacuum may be real for a reason: restaurants do not pay for software, and everyone who looked at this before concluded the same. That is why the sixty-pound question has a kill date, and why the wholesaler is the pivot rather than a footnote.

We are not building anything the diner sees, which annoys the marketing manager who wants a QR allergen menu and has been asking for one since the pandemic. We are not selling to single sites, which annoys the single-site chef who would love this and cannot pay for it, and we are not chasing chains, which annoys whoever does our sales, because the logo they want is a compliance department with a bespoke system. We are not doing nutrition, calories or costing, which annoys the ops director who wants one tool for everything. We are not letting the software answer "is this safe for me", which annoys the investor who wants that demo. We are not building for the chef, meaning no recipe editing and no nice kitchen features, which annoys the chef, who will experience this as a thing done to them, and that is a cost we are accepting on purpose. We are not letting the owner edit history, which annoys the owner, our buyer, the first time they want to tidy the ledger before an inspection; that is the one annoyance we must never resolve. And we are not going to the wholesaler yet, which will annoy the account manager who can see the upside faster than we can.

Headline: Restaurant groups can now show what was in any dish on any day. Subhead: Fourteen keeps a restaurant's allergen sheet true from the moment a delivery arrives, and keeps the proof. Body: When a wholesaler swaps one pesto for another, the allergens in a dish can change before the kitchen has finished unpacking. Until now the only record was a laminated sheet that was right the day it was printed. With Fourteen, the person who signs for the delivery photographs the note, any dish affected by a substitution is marked on the floor within minutes, the chef confirms it with one look at what changed, and the sheet at every site reprints itself. Every change is kept with a name and a time, and nothing can be edited afterwards, so when an inspector or an insurer asks what was true on a Thursday in June, the answer is one tap. Quote, from the owner of a six-site group: "For years the only thing standing between a diner and a mistake was whether the right chef happened to be on that night. Now I can show anyone what we knew and when we knew it." Getting started: import the menu from the costing system, set the group's may-contain rule once, and hand the porter a phone. Sixty pounds a site a month.

Value: the customer and the user are different people, so it is two answers. The owner buys it if the record is worth sixty pounds a site, which is the kill test in December and unproven. The users are three: the porter will use it if it is one photo and nothing else; the chef will use it grudgingly, because it watches them; the waiter uses nothing new, they read the same laminate. Usability: three unproven moments. A photo at seven with wet hands and a folded note; a chef confirmation that must show what changed in one glance, not a list of flags, or it becomes the Monday click ritual from the premortem; and entering a special at the pass in under a minute, which nobody has designed yet. Feasibility: the append-only ledger and the reprint are boring, known work; the risk is the matching layer between the wholesaler's product names and our recipes, and reading bad photographs; two people for six weeks is enough for the spine if the spike on matching runs first. Viability: sixty pounds times six sites is three hundred and sixty a month per group, so a real business needs a few hundred groups, which exist, reached through brokers we have not yet signed. Two things sit under that. We hold a record for years, so retention and who can see across groups are our problem now. And if our record is ever unfaithful, we are the ones in the witness box, so we need our own cover before the first site goes live.

No. The bet is six weeks for the spine at two sites: photo in, ledger entry, dishes flagged, laminate reprinted. If that is not running at both sites on the last Friday, the bet expires and the team goes to cooldown; it does not get another six weeks because it is nearly there, because nearly there is what the two sites' last tool said. Before it gets to that point the scope hammer applies in the order already agreed: spec-sheet reading goes first, automatic reprint becomes a print button second, the ledger never. The one exception I will allow in advance, so nobody has to argue for it on the day: if the spine is live end to end at one site and the second site is only waiting on its menu import, that finishes in cooldown, capped at two weeks, and it is the only thing that does. If what is missing is the matching layer, that is not an extension case at all; it means the spike was wrong, and the bet gets reshaped and re-pitched, not stretched.

The thing that goes up with value is verified days: days on which every dish on a site's wall was confirmed against the last substitution before service. That is what the owner is buying and what the insurer would care about, and it is what we should report on the first screen. But we should not meter on it, because charging more for being diligent is backwards, and we must never charge per change or per photo, because that taxes the capture step we are begging the porter to do. So the unit an owner will accept paying more for is the site, with a tier by live dishes: a site with two hundred dishes and Saturday specials carries more risk and gets more from us than a twenty-dish bistro, and owners understand that without explanation. Sites times menu size is the price; verified days is the number that tells us, and them, whether the price is earning its keep. If verified days at a site sit under ninety percent for a quarter, that site is churning whether the owner has noticed or not.

Never asked directly, and that is the honest headline. The sixty pounds is built from three things: the tool the two sites abandoned was about thirty-five a site, the head chef's Monday rebuild is roughly three hours a week, which at kitchen rates is around a hundred and eighty pounds a site a month of chef time, and I would pay a hundred myself for the record after that Thursday in June, but I am the one person whose answer does not count. By feature, my guess before asking: the record with a name and a time is the only thing the owner pays for; the self-reprinting laminate is worth something to the site manager and nothing to the owner; spec-sheet reading is what the chef wants and what nobody upstairs will pay a penny for; the diner-facing menu would come from the marketing budget, which is why it is out of bounds. What we will do about it: five owners in September, each asked at what price this is too cheap to trust, a bargain, expensive, and out of the question, before we hear the number they'd like to hear; and one broker asked what a verified record is worth on a premium, in writing. Until then, sixty is a placeholder with a kill date, not a price.

Everything that could be asked "what did you know and when" about. The delivery-note photo as taken, with its hash, and the substitution line we read from it, with the model version that read it. The spec sheet as received, the file and the email it arrived in. Every change to a dish's status: before, after, who confirmed, when, and how long it sat unverified. The may-contain policy in force at that moment, as a version, because a dish's status only makes sense against the rule of the day. Every print: which version went on which wall at which site at what time, as the actual PDF, since the sheet on the wall is what the waiter read. Menu imports, and the eval result for every release. Not in it, ever: anything about a diner. No names, no reactions, no health information; the restaurant's ticket note is theirs, and the moment we hold diner data the product is a different product. How long: a claim for injury in England runs three years from the date of knowledge, contract and negligence six, and there is no limit on a manslaughter charge, so six years from the day of the entry, and the owner cannot shorten it; our solicitor confirms the number before the first site goes live. Storage for six years of photographs is a cost we price in, not a surprise.

Nobody migrates, because there is nothing to migrate to; we sit beside everything and change one thing, which is what counts as the record. The laminate stays on the wall and we print it. The binder stays for the inspector who wants paper, and every month we print the ledger extract into it. The costing system stays the master for dishes and we import from it one way, again at every menu change, never writing back. The EPOS allergen field is left exactly as it is, declared in writing to be not the record, because trying to fix it would spend the cycle. WhatsApp carries on; the porter's photo goes to us, and if the sous chef posts it in the group too, fine. The spreadsheet is the one thing that has to die visibly, and we cannot kill it from the software: the owner's allergen policy names Fourteen as the record, the printed sheet carries our version stamp, and any laminate on a wall without a stamp is the site manager's problem at the monthly check. The two-year risk is two truths on two walls; the stamp and the policy are the whole defence, and the monthly check is where we find out if it is holding.

The date is the thirtieth of June 2027, ten months from now and six months after the December gates. The state is five numbers, all of them or I quit. Twenty groups paying full price, not pilots, not discounts. Capture above eighty percent at every live site for the trailing quarter, measured from the wholesaler's own substitution log, not our count. Verified days above ninety percent across all sites for that quarter. One broker who has put a verified record into a policy term in writing. And zero occasions where our ledger was shown to be unfaithful, meaning it displayed something other than what was entered. If any of the five is missing on that day, the restaurant product stops. What we have learned about wholesalers and matching goes into one conversation with a wholesaler, and if that conversation does not turn into a paid pilot by the end of September 2027, the company closes.

Two of them can, and one of them is the trap. Verified days goes up on its own the moment chefs learn the Monday click: confirm everything unread and the site reads a hundred percent while the wall is wrong, which is the premortem in a number. So a confirmation only counts if the chef opened the change, and we report the time from substitution to confirmation as a distribution, not an average; a site that confirms everything at nine on Monday shows up as a spike, not as diligence. Capture rate is measured against the wholesaler's own log, so it does not drift up by itself, but it gets easier if the wholesaler substitutes less, so absolute substitutions per site sit next to it. Paying groups only moves with effort. The number that goes up beautifully when we do nothing is days since an incident, and it is the one every owner will want on the front screen. We never show it. It was going up for years before that Thursday in June

The failures run in the wrong order: the cheap ones are visible and the dangerous ones are not. A false positive, a dish flagged for an allergen it does not contain, is visible within the hour because the chef sees it, and it costs one confirmation and a diner turned away from a dish they could have eaten; the price is trust, because a chef who sees three of those stops reading the flags. A false negative, a missed "contains" on a spec sheet, is invisible until a diner reacts, and there may be months between the two. A match failure, a substitution that reaches no dish, is invisible in the same way. An unreadable photo that nobody bounces back is a substitution that never happened as far as the ledger knows. So the design's job is to make the invisible ones visible: unmatched lines surface as unverified rather than disappearing, an unreadable photo goes straight back to the porter's phone, and every week a second chef re-checks a sample of dishes the system says are confirmed, which is the only check that can catch a missed "contains" before a diner does. Who pays for a wrong answer, in order: the diner with their body, the waiter and the chef with their jobs, the owner in court, and us in the witness box explaining the model version. The order never changes; the design only changes how long the queue is.

Thin, and I should list it rather than describe it. One near-miss on one night at one site, which is an anecdote. One WhatsApp thread and one stale spreadsheet, which are evidence of the process, not of demand. Two sites that abandoned a rival tool, which is evidence that the chef-in-the-loop design fails, not that ours succeeds. My own willingness to pay, which does not count. Zero owner interviews, zero brokers in writing, zero inspectors in writing, and no capture data at all. Set against the consequence, it is proportionate for what we are about to spend and not for what we are about to risk. Spending four weeks on a capture test, a week on a matching spike, and five conversations with owners is cheap enough to do on an anecdote, and each of those turns an opinion into a number. Putting a self-printing sheet on a wall that a waiter will trust more than the old one is not cheap, and the evidence for doing that has to be of a different kind: an eval with zero missed "contains" on our own suppliers' sheets, a chef's confirmation before any print, and a second chef re-checking a sample every week. So the honest position is this: we have enough to learn, not enough to ship, and the gates in the last twenty-nine answers are the difference between the two.
